findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Dockerfile:3 downloads bytes from a mutable remote endpoint and pipes them directly to sh during every image build. A compromised or changed endpoint can execute arbitrary commands in the build and alter the resulting image.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Dockerfile:3 downloads and pipes remote content directly to `sh`. Content served by that URL can execute arbitrary commands as root during every image build.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This changed line downloads a script at build time and pipes it directly to sh without a pinned version, checksum, or signature. A changed or compromised remote response executes arbitrary code during image creation and can backdoor the shipped image.

findings.title: Make installer download failures fail the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline returns sh's status. If curl fails before writing script content, sh can exit successfully after consuming an empty stream, allowing the image build to succeed without the requested installation.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key signal
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but the new exported LoadOrDefault discards that error and returns "", which is also a valid stored map value. Callers cannot distinguish an absent key from a stored empty value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures in the exported helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards that error and returns "", making a missing key indistinguishable from a present key whose legitimate value is empty.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key status in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported function explicitly discards Load's ErrMissing result, returning "" for both an absent key and a key stored with an empty value. Callers therefore cannot distinguish missing data from a legitimate empty value.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: The new untracked goroutines allow Run to return before any or all sends execute. This changes the synchronous completion behavior: a caller can observe incomplete results when Run returns, and closing a caller-owned results channel at that boundary can panic in a delayed goroutine.

findings.title: Wait for all result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: The new untracked goroutine at the changed lines lets Run return before results are sent. A caller that closes results after Run returns can trigger a later send-on-closed-channel panic, and callers can no longer rely on completed processing when Run returns.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each job send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run returns immediately. A caller that assumes return means all results have been sent can close or stop consuming results, causing missing results or a send-on-closed-channel panic.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant ownership for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `||` allows a non-admin session in the record's tenant to delete it, and allows an admin from a different tenant to delete it. The prior implementation required both conditions.

findings.title: Require admin status before allowing record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `||` returns true for a non-admin session whose tenant matches the record, whereas the prior predicate required both admin status and tenant matching. This authorizes deletion by non-admin tenant users.

findings.title: Keep deletion authorization constrained to the record tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || authorizes an admin from any other tenant to delete this record, and authorizes every non-admin user in the same tenant. The previous predicate required both administrative privilege and matching tenant, so this is a tenant-isolation and authorization bypass.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of resetting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or partially invalid saved settings previously threw, preventing updateFontSize from writing. They now become DEFAULTS, so updateFontSize overwrites all valid fields such as a user's theme with "light" while saving the requested font size.

findings.title: Preserve invalid-settings errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The new empty catch converts malformed JSON and schema-validation failures into DEFAULTS. updateFontSize then changes that default object and calls save, overwriting a corrupt or incompatible settings payload; previously JSON.parse or validation errors stopped save from running.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of silently resetting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid settings now return a valid-looking default object. updateFontSize then changes its font size and saves it, overwriting the user's prior settings instead of surfacing the invalid input.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When `branch` and `verified` resolve to different commits, `builtFrom` identifies the requested branch commit while `artifacts` are loaded from the verified commit, producing a self-inconsistent `BuildReport`.

findings.title: Keep artifacts aligned with builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", the report declares builtFrom as the branch commit while returning artifacts from the verified commit. Consumers can therefore display, deploy, or audit artifacts as though they were produced by the reported branch when they were not.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` is set to `build.ref(branch)`, while `artifacts` are loaded with `build.ref("verified")`. If those refs differ, the returned report identifies one commit but contains artifacts from another.

findings.title: Apply the requested positive limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For limit > 0, the function returns the entire reversed input instead of at most limit entries. renderFeed calls it with 20 and copies every returned entry, so inputs over 20 entries produce output over 20 entries.

findings.title: Preserve the positive limit when returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns the complete reversed input rather than at most limit entries. renderFeed passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9; with more than 20 entries, its loop writes past the intended 20-item page and returns all entries.

findings.title: Apply the positive limit before returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For a positive limit smaller than all.length, recentEntries returns every reversed entry. renderFeed passes 20, then writes each returned item into a 20-slot array; indexes beyond 19 extend the array, so feeds over 20 entries return more than 20 items.

findings.title: Count only entries emitted in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: When an entry has `stale=true`, its row is removed but `# entry-count` still uses `entries.length`. Consumers receive a header count that does not match the emitted rows.

findings.title: Count only rendered entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: Stale entries are now omitted from output rows, but the header still receives entries.length. The emitted # entry-count can therefore exceed the number of manifest rows.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed filter omits stale entries from manifest rows, but the returned header still uses entries.length. A manifest with stale entries therefore declares more entries than it emits.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was exported from this module before this change, but is no longer exported. Existing consumers importing it from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed module no longer exports shippingQuote. Existing TypeScript or JavaScript consumers importing it from src/orders will fail to resolve the export.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed module no longer exports `shippingQuote`; consumers importing that named export from `src/orders` will fail to type-check or load after upgrading.

findings.title: Restore execute's successful result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to execute now throws "always fails" instead of returning the uppercase input, making the module's sole public operation unusable.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the public execute(input): string API now throws "always fails"; no input can produce the declared result. This is a complete regression from the prior uppercase transformation.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute function now throws "always fails"; previously it returned the input uppercased, so all consumers lose the function's only behavior.

findings.title: Preserve the read-only viewer path
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `req.role === "viewer"` rejection runs before `handle`'s viewer branch at src/handler.ts:24, so active viewers below the attempt limit now receive "rejected" rather than "read-only".

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: This makes isEligible false for every viewer, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24 and can no longer reach its explicit "read-only" result at line 25. Before this change, an active viewer with fewer than five attempts received "read-only".

findings.title: Allow eligible viewers to reach the read-only handler
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, the new condition makes isEligible return false, so handle returns "rejected" rather than reaching its viewer-specific "read-only" result.

findings.title: Stop requiring payment to save a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: For `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }`, the new predicate returns false. `src/actions.ts:9` therefore returns "blocked", whereas it previously returned "saved". Payment governs submission, but not persisting a draft.

findings.title: Keep payment status out of draft saving
findings.whyItBreaks: The new payment conjunct makes unpaid drafts fail canProceed, so saveDraft returns "blocked" at src/actions.ts:9 rather than "saved".

findings.title: Keep unpaid drafts saveable
findings.whyItBreaks: The new payment predicate returns false for a draft with payment="missing". saveDraft uses canProceed as its gate at src/actions.ts:9, so saving that draft returns "blocked" even though payment is only relevant to submission.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, publishSnapshot returns commit=repo.headCommit(channel) while files come from repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable")). Consumers receive an internally inconsistent snapshot and can publish stable's content labeled as the requested channel's commit.

findings.title: Read files from the published channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from `stable`, the returned Snapshot.commit identifies the channel head while Snapshot.files describes a different commit. Consumers cannot reliably retrieve the files belonging to the reported snapshot.

findings.title: Keep snapshot files aligned with the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot.commit identifies that channel's head but Snapshot.files are read from stable. Consumers cannot reconstruct or publish the reported commit and receive unrelated content.

findings.title: Honor the advertised limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Callers can now request a specific limit, but the function always uses max_count = 10 and returns ten entries. This makes the public parameter's promised result-affecting behavior unusable.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Calling build("item", 1) still returns 10 entries because the body continues to iterate over the hard-coded max_count=10. Callers cannot obtain the limit promised by the new parameter.

findings.title: Honor the limit argument
findings.whyItBreaks: build("item", 2) still returns 10 values because the body always sets max_count to 10. The added public parameter therefore promises caller-controlled output size but has no observable effect.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly named parse_positive_int('-1') returns -1; its changed consumer at src/validators.py:6 then makes charge('-1') return -100. The new API contract therefore does not validate positivity.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new name promises a positive integer, but the changed function still returns int(value), accepting 0 and negative inputs. charge() directly consumes that result and returns zero or negative cent amounts instead of rejecting invalid amounts.

findings.title: Validate positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('-2') returns -2 because its body only calls int(). The new public name promises a positive result, and charge converts that value into a negative cents value.

findings.title: Preserve the caller’s DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the function updated and returned a copy, leaving df unchanged. It now writes directly to df, so callers that retain the input as an unmodified baseline will silently observe mapped values in both the input and returned result.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed df.copy() means applying any non-empty mapping overwrites values in the DataFrame supplied by the caller. Previously the function returned a transformed copy while preserving the input, so callers that reuse the source DataFrame now observe unintended changed values.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed loop writes directly through df.loc and returns df. Callers that retain the input will now observe it modified, whereas the base implementation updated and returned an independent copy.

findings.title: Restore or implement the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int` is newly named as though it guarantees a positive result, but negative and zero numeric inputs pass through unchanged. The changed caller `charge` therefore returns negative or zero cents for those inputs.

findings.title: Validate positivity before returning the parsed value
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1` despite its new positive-only contract. The changed in-file caller at `src/parse.rs:6` multiplies that result, so `charge("-1")` returns `-100` instead of rejecting or mapping the invalid amount.

findings.title: Validate the positive-int contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1`, despite its newly introduced positive-result contract; the in-file consumer then produces a negative charge (`-100`).

findings.title: Avoid moving items before computing its length
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and returns `items` by value, moving the `Vec<String>`. The subsequent `items.len()` therefore borrows a moved value and fails compilation.

findings.title: Borrow items for debug output
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and returns `items`, which is then discarded by the semicolon. This moves the Vec before `items.len()` on line 3, causing Rust error E0382 (borrow of moved value).

findings.title: Avoid moving items before computing its length
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` consumes the `Vec<String>` and discards its returned value; `items.len()` on line 3 then uses a moved value, causing Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Compute paths from the returned base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Changeset contract says changedPaths are computed against fromRevision and replayed on that revision. The changed line instead computes paths from latest while returning the pinned-tag revision as fromRevision, producing an inconsistent changeset.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Changeset contract says changedPaths are computed against fromRevision and replayed on that revision. This change resolves latest separately, then computes changedPaths from latest while returning the pinned revision as fromRevision, producing an invalid changeset when they differ.

findings.title: Compute paths from the advertised base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `Changeset.fromRevision` promises the revision used to compute `changedPaths`, but the changed line reads paths from `latest` while returning the pinned revision. A consumer replaying these paths on `fromRevision` can apply paths from the wrong revision.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql:1 still executes `SELECT email FROM users`; deployments applying the migration will receive a missing-column SQL error.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`; that query will fail with a missing-column error on migrated databases.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users. Executing that query after migration fails with a missing-column database error.

findings.title: Restore environment-based billing credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line embeds a live-form billing key in source control, exposing it to repository readers. It also makes exported makeClient() return a usable client when BILLING_API_KEY is absent, replacing the previous explicit configuration error.

findings.title: Remove and rotate the hard-coded live billing key
findings.whyItBreaks: A `bk_live_` credential is now committed to source control, exposing billing API access to anyone with repository or build-log access.

findings.title: Preserve failure when the billing credential is unset
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously an unset BILLING_API_KEY threw an error; the exported makeClient now always returns a client with a fixed key, so external callers cannot detect missing deployment configuration.

findings.title: Restore environment-based billing key validation
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line embeds a `bk_live_` billing key in tracked source and makes exported `makeClient()` return it for every deployment. This exposes the credential to repository readers and build artifacts, prevents per-deployment key selection or rotation, and converts a missing-secret startup failure into authenticated billing requests.

findings.title: Restore the admin authorization requirement for purging
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed branch returns "forbidden" when user.isAdmin is true. A non-admin with an archived project passes both guards and reaches db.delete(project.id), permitting unauthorized permanent deletion.

findings.title: Restore the administrator authorization guard
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guard returns "forbidden" for administrators, then permits any non-admin user to delete an archived project. This reverses the previous behavior, which allowed only administrators to purge archived projects.

findings.title: Restore the admin authorization check before deleting
findings.whyItBreaks: For an archived project, `user.isAdmin === false` now passes both guards and calls `db.delete`, while an administrator is always returned "forbidden". This reverses the prior authorization policy and permits unauthorized project deletion.

findings.title: Restore fallback when the settings file is missing
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path (app/config.py:6-7), and the changed startup code indexes settings["workers"] at line 14. This raises TypeError instead of returning the previous default worker count of 1.

findings.title: Preserve defaults when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path (app/config.py:6-7). Without the removed fallback, startup evaluates settings["workers"] on None and raises TypeError, breaking the previously supported no-settings-file startup path.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-file settings default
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path, while the changed startup code immediately indexes settings["workers"]. An absent settings file therefore raises TypeError instead of returning the previous one-worker default.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error and returns nil. Its exported API now forces callers to conflate a failed payment with a successful one, allowing them to proceed with success handling despite no charge being submitted.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge logs it and returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a failed charge from a completed charge and may proceed as though payment succeeded.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, exported Charge logs the error and returns nil. Callers therefore receive a success result even though gateway submission failed.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A fetches a setting named "theme", the cache stores it as "settings:theme". A later settingsFor call for tenant B with the same name returns the cached value before calling store.fetch, leaking tenant-specific configuration.

findings.title: Include tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor fetches values using tenantId, but its changed cache key includes only name. Once tenant A caches a setting, tenant B requesting the same name receives tenant A's value without calling store.fetch.

findings.title: Include tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: `settingsFor` now derives its key solely from `name`. After one tenant caches a setting, another tenant requesting the same name receives that cached value without calling `store.fetch` for its own tenant.

findings.title: Preserve invalidate's tenant-scoped public API
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function changed from `invalidate(tenantId, name)` to `invalidate(name)`. Existing TypeScript consumers using the documented exported signature fail to compile; JavaScript consumers passing two arguments invalidate the tenant ID as a setting name instead of the requested setting.

findings.title: Serialize reservations across the asynchronous save
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent calls with one unit both read `remaining === 1` before either awaited save completes. Both save zero, both return true, and two orders are accepted for one item. The prior synchronous implementation completed the in-memory decrement before another call could observe the old stock.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await yields before stock is decremented. With stock=1, two concurrent calls can both read remaining=1, both save 0, both set stock to 0, and both return true—successfully reserving two units from one available unit.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for each SKU before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent reserve("sku") calls with stock=1 both read remaining=1 before either reaches the post-await stock update. Both save 0 and return true, so one unit is reserved twice.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still multiplies its result by 1,000. The first failed attempt therefore sleeps 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 minutes) instead of 1,000 ms.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 ms, but `retry` still passes `backoff(a) * 1000` to its millisecond `sleep` helper. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1 second; capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed backoff value is now milliseconds, but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still multiplies it by 1,000 before passing it to sleep. Its first retry waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1,000 ms.

findings.title: Propagate the file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The new deferred Close discards its return value. Save therefore returns nil after a successful Flush even when the final file close fails, weakening this exported function's public error result.

findings.title: Propagate file close failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The new deferred `f.Close()` discards its error. Previously, after a successful flush, Save returned `f.Close()`, allowing callers to detect close-time write or filesystem failures; it now returns nil instead.

findings.title: Return the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The new deferred Close result is discarded, so exported Save returns nil after a successful Flush even if closing the created file fails. The base implementation returned that error to callers.

findings.title: Include the page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds helper returns a half-open end, but range(start, end - 1) excludes the final valid index. A two-row page returns only its first row; a one-row page returns no rows. render_page and summarize therefore omit the last row of every page.

findings.title: Include the page endpoint in the window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) bounds, but range(start, end - 1) stops at end - 2. Each non-empty page loses its final row; single-row pages become empty, including through summarize.

findings.title: Include the page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds helper defines end as exclusive, but range(start, end - 1) stops one element early. Thus page_window(["a", "b"], 0, 2) returns only ["a"], and render_page at lib/pagination.py:40 and summarize at lib/pagination.py:56 silently omit the last row of each page.

findings.title: Return entries only while their TTL is still valid
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison is inverted: a newly stored entry has age near zero and is deleted as a cache miss, while an entry older than ttlMs is returned as valid.

findings.title: Remove completed jobs without splicing during iteration
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing shifts the next job into an index that `forEach` has already passed. For example, `[done, done, pending]` returns `[done, pending]`, so completed jobs remain.

findings.title: Return entries before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age near zero, so `age > ttlMs` is false and it is deleted/returned as null. Once expired, the same condition becomes true and the stale value is returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove every completed job without mutating the input
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during `forEach` shifts the next element into the current index, then `forEach` advances past it. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second completed job remains. This also changes the prior contract by mutating the caller's `jobs` array.

findings.title: Return cache entries before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has an age near zero, so `age > ttlMs` is false and `get()` deletes it immediately. Conversely, entries older than the TTL are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice the array while iterating with forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next job into the current index, but `forEach` advances to the following index. For example, `[done, done, pending]` returns `[done, pending]`, leaving a completed job unpruned.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() compares numbers as strings. For scores [100, 9, 8], it produces [100, 8, 9], then reverse() yields [9, 8, 100]. With n=1, cutoff becomes 9, so topPlayers can include a 9-point player and slice it ahead of the 100-point player based on input order.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before computing the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores 9, 80, and 100 with n=1, rankScores produces [9, 80, 100], making the cutoff 9 and causing topPlayers to return the 9-score player instead of the 100-score player.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before reversing
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores 9 and 100, rankScores returns [9, 100], causing topPlayers(..., 1) to use 9 as its cutoff and select the lower-scoring player.

findings.title: Use constant-time comparison for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed equality comparison can return after the first mismatched character, exposing an authentication timing oracle. `handle` invokes `processor(payload)` only after `verify` accepts the signature, so a forged signature reaches webhook processing.

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `==` comparison can return earlier for mismatches near the beginning of the HMAC, exposing prefix-dependent timing during authentication. An attacker able to make repeated requests may use this signal to guess a valid signature.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Normal string equality can stop at the first mismatch, exposing a timing signal based on the matching HMAC prefix. Repeated webhook requests could use this to forge a signature; the prior hmac.compare_digest comparison avoided that leak.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits when line 23 exits its `with` block, before line 24 applies either account update. If an update fails, the ledger row persists even though balances are unchanged or only the source account was debited.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance changes in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits the ledger insert before `_apply_balances` runs. If either balance update fails, a durable ledger entry remains; if the second update fails, the source may also be debited without crediting the destination.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits after `_record_ledger` at line 24, before `_apply_balances` runs. A failure in either subsequent account UPDATE can therefore leave a committed ledger row with no balance mutation, or with only the debit applied.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed return expression uses local-time getters, so the same instant can produce different billing keys depending on the server timezone. For example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 on a UTC-08 host, splitting billing-day comparisons and keys.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed return expression uses the process host's local date. At 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z, a server in America/Los_Angeles returns 2025-12-31 rather than 2026-01-01, so identical billing events can be assigned to different billing days depending on deployment timezone.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed call at line 4 uses local-time getters. An instant such as 2026-08-17T00:30:00Z becomes 2026-08-16 on a host in America/Los_Angeles, while the base implementation produced the UTC key 2026-08-17. Billing-day grouping and sameBillingDay therefore vary by deployment timezone.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants using the same account ID share one memo entry. After tenant A's profile is cached, readProfile for tenant B returns tenant A's Profile without calling fetchProfile.

findings.title: Include tenant in the memoization key
findings.whyItBreaks: After a request caches account "A" for tenant T1, a request for account "A" in T2 returns T1's cached Profile at line 16 and never calls fetchProfile. This exposes incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads account `alice`, a read for tenant B and account `alice` returns the cached tenant-A Profile without calling fetchProfile. Profile includes a tenant field, so this leaks tenant-specific profile data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch converts the explicit missing-key error into "", making an absent key indistinguishable from a stored empty string. Both the exported `load` API and `loadAll` callers receive a successful result instead of the prior failure.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors instead of returning an empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch converts the missing-key Error into "", making absent values indistinguishable from stored empty strings. The in-file `loadAll` consumer consequently returns successful-looking arrays for incomplete data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed catch converts a missing key from `Error("missing: <key>")` into `""`, a valid Map value. `src/store.ts:12` loadAll maps that fallback into its returned string array, so incomplete data is indistinguishable from legitimate empty values.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config timeout contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers pass Config as `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }`. They now fail TypeScript excess-property/missing-property checks; already-built JavaScript callers supply no `timeout`, so `Date.now() + undefined` becomes NaN and the deadline guard never stops retries.

findings.title: Make retryBackground run outside the caller's stack
findings.whyItBreaks: `retryBackground` invokes `fn()` directly before returning, so a slow or blocking function blocks its caller exactly like `retry`; the exported name promises background execution that the implementation does not provide.

findings.title: Expose terminal retryBackground failures
findings.whyItBreaks: After all retries fail, the catch path returns `void`, identical to successful completion. As a public API, this forces every caller to conflate an exhausted failure with success and can cause failed background work to be treated as completed.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing timeoutMs with required retries and timeout breaks existing TypeScript Config objects. JavaScript callers still passing timeoutMs supply undefined for config.timeout, making the deadline NaN and disabling timeout enforcement.

findings.title: Make retryBackground actually run off the foreground path
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly exported background API synchronously invokes fn and retries in its caller's execution path before returning. Slow or failing work therefore blocks the caller.

findings.title: Expose exhaustion failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty catch discards every failure and the function returns void after retries are exhausted, indistinguishable from a successful completion.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing Config fields
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript consumers using `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer type-check because `timeoutMs` was removed and unrelated `retries` is required. JavaScript consumers passing the prior shape get `config.timeout === undefined`, making the deadline `NaN`; the timeout guard then never stops retries.

findings.title: Propagate terminal failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: When every callback attempt throws, this new exported function catches each exception and returns normally after the loop. Callers cannot distinguish successful completion from exhausted failure.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now accepts numbers, but the changed render path reads `value.length`. A caller passing `42` receives `len=undefined`, and TypeScript rejects accessing `length` on `string | number`.

findings.title: Render the supplied field value rather than its length
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously `<Field value="abc" />` displayed `abc`; it now displays `len=3`. This silently changes the value users edit for every existing string caller.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now publicly accepts `number`, but `number` has no `length` property. TypeScript rejects this expression; if emitted without type checking, `<Field value={12} />` produces `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed exported prop type permits numeric values, while the changed implementation interpolates `value.length`. A numeric value therefore produces `len=undefined` instead of a meaningful input value.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. The same helper reads the complete stdout of `git diff` at line 140, so a PR whose textual diff exceeds that limit makes spawnSync fail and the outer handler reports a failed review instead of reviewing the PR. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these inputs.

findings.title: Restore sufficient buffer capacity for Git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. This helper produces the complete PR patch at line 140, so any PR whose textual diff exceeds that limit causes Git to terminate with a buffer error and the review job to fail instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. This helper captures the complete `git diff` output at src/adapters/github.ts:140, so a larger patch causes git collection to fail and runGithub posts a failed check instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Restore the explicit read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed argv omits `-s read-only`, so `codex exec` can use ambient sandbox/trust configuration. Since it runs with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and receives the review prompt as input, a workspace-write configuration permits modification of the repository under review.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex runs Codex with `opts.repoPath` as its working directory. Removing `-s read-only` permits the review agent to modify the supplied checkout, despite this wrapper being used for review execution.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting `-s read-only` delegates sandbox policy to Codex configuration/defaults, allowing a review invocation to run write-capable commands in `opts.repoPath` and modify the inspected repository.

findings.title: Diff the PR head from its merge-base
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is a newer base-branch commit that is not an ancestor of the PR head, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes base-branch changes after the branch point. Needlefish then reviews and classifies unrelated files; the prior code computed the merge-base before producing both values.

findings.title: Diff from the PR merge-base, not the current base tip
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current base-branch tip and that branch has advanced since the PR branch diverged, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes reverse changes from the base branch as if they belonged to the PR. The review bundle and `changedPaths` then cover unrelated files, so the agent can review and post inline findings against files not changed by the PR. The prior merge-base calculation excluded those base-only commits.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences when interpolating prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets `$&`, `$'`, `$`` and `$$` in string replacements. Bundle data and patches can contain these source-text sequences, so the changed replacements can corrupt the review or critic prompt before it is passed to runCodex.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences in injected prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in string replacement values. A patch, bundle, or candidate finding containing these sequences is altered before the assembled prompt is passed to runCodex; the prior callback replacements preserved it literally.

findings.title: Preserve bundle text during prompt interpolation
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed replacement argument is interpreted by `String.prototype.replace`. A `$&`, `$`` or `$'` sequence in serialized bundle content—such as the patch—will be expanded instead of inserted literally, corrupting the review prompt.

findings.title: Preserve critic inputs during prompt interpolation
findings.whyItBreaks: Candidate findings and `bundle.patch` are passed as replacement strings. `$&`, `$`` and `$'` sequences are expanded by `replace`, so the critic can receive corrupted findings or patch content.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: If the primary review submission fails and the PR advances before the fallback request, the omitted commit_id lets GitHub attach the fallback review to the latest commit. Its body and verdict were generated from the earlier headSha, so unreviewed code can receive that review result.

findings.title: Preserve the reviewed commit in fallback submissions
findings.whyItBreaks: When the full review request fails, the fallback omits commit_id. GitHub defaults that field to the PR's latest commit, while the review result was generated from headSha. If a commit is pushed during review, the fallback can attach the result to unreviewed code.

findings.title: Preserve the reviewed commit in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary request is pinned to headSha, but if it fails and a new commit is pushed before the fallback runs, omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the review to the PR's then-latest commit. The review result and check run were computed for the original headSha, so a REQUEST_CHANGES review can incorrectly block newer code that was never reviewed.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating P1 bugs
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid finding fields such as severity "P9" or a missing file/lineStart are now returned by normalizeReview as a P1/bug finding with an empty file and line 0. Callers cannot distinguish that malformed review output from a real P1 finding.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating P1s
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid findings now normalize to a P1/bug result with fallback or empty required fields. For example, an invalid severity becomes P1 and missing location fields become an empty file and line 0, so callers receive an actionable-looking review finding rather than a malformed-output error.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of emitting defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or incomplete review data no longer raises a malformed-output error. A finding missing required fields is emitted as a valid-looking P1/bug finding with an empty file and line 0, while invalid severity/category values are silently reclassified. Callers cannot distinguish malformed input from a real finding.

findings.title: Keep explicit repository routing for manual PR resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these gh pr view calls run before actions/checkout. With neither -R nor GH_REPO, gh has no repository context on a clean runner and the ref-resolution step fails; checkout therefore never receives the requested PR head.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository for manual PR ref lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so lines 38-39 execute before actions/checkout. Removing -R means gh pr view must derive its repository from the working directory's Git remote (or GH_REPO); a fresh self-hosted runner workspace has neither checkout nor configured repository context. The commands therefore cannot resolve the PR SHAs, leaving the subsequent checkout without the requested head ref.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository when resolving dispatched PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so execution reaches lines 38-39 before actions/checkout at .github/workflows/review.yml:42. The changed gh pr view commands no longer receive a repository and there is no checked-out Git repository from which gh can infer one, so the advertised manual PR review cannot resolve its head/base SHAs.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null, {}, or a response with findings/checked/residual_risks of the wrong type previously threw, allowing callers to treat the review as failed. They now become an empty summary with no findings and no blocking residual risks, so the exported API forces callers to conflate malformed reviewer output with a legitimate clean review.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output instead of returning an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Undefined, non-object, or incomplete review output previously threw a malformed-output error. The changed code instead returns a valid-looking empty review, making parser/LLM failures indistinguishable from a legitimate no-findings result.

findings.title: Preserve malformed review-output failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs that previously threw (for example null, a missing findings array, or a non-string summary) now return a valid RawReview with empty/default fields. Because normalizeReview is exported, callers are forced to conflate a failed/malformed review response with a genuine review reporting no findings or risks.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, pull_request context is absent. This fallback checks out github.ref—the ref used to dispatch the workflow—rather than the PR selected by inputs.pr_number. The base-ref fallback also uses main, while PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are empty, so dispatching a review for a PR with another base can analyze the wrong revision or run without the requested SHA bounds.

findings.title: Restore PR-ref resolution for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The changed PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA expressions therefore pass empty values, while the checkout at line 29 falls back to github.ref—the dispatch branch rather than the requested pr_number’s head. Manual runs review the wrong revision.

findings.title: Resolve the manually selected PR before running the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, the pull_request payload is absent. The new expressions therefore check out github.ref, fetch main, and pass empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA, ignoring the required pr_number. A manual review can consequently analyze the dispatch branch instead of the selected PR.

findings.title: Preserve a buffer large enough for review diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `spawnSync` call no longer sets `maxBuffer`, so Node applies its 1 MiB default. `runLocal` passes the complete `git diff baseSha HEAD` output through this helper at `src/adapters/local.ts:100`; diffs over that limit cause the git invocation to fail and the review to throw.

findings.title: Retain capacity for large Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `spawnSync` defaults `maxBuffer` to 1 MiB. `runLocal` obtains the full review patch through this helper at line 100, so any diff exceeding that size terminates the Git process with a buffer error and aborts the review instead of passing the patch to `review`. The previous 64 MiB limit explicitly supported these inputs.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for review diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` reads the complete `git diff` through this helper at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, Node's `spawnSync` default is 1 MiB; larger PR diffs cause the command to exceed that buffer and throw rather than producing a review.

findings.title: Keep review failures blocking
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or review posting throws, the catch path creates a neutral check even though its summary states that the PR did not pass. A neutral GitHub check satisfies required-check gating, so a required Needlefish check no longer blocks a PR when review execution fails.

findings.title: Report review failures as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, this path posts the fixed Needlefish check with conclusion "neutral" despite reporting that the review did not pass. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-check conclusion, so a branch rule requiring Needlefish can permit merging without a completed review.

findings.title: Report review errors as failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When review execution throws, this posts a completed `neutral` Needlefish check. GitHub accepts neutral conclusions for required checks, so a PR whose review never completed can satisfy the Needlefish gate despite the error message explicitly saying it did not pass.

findings.title: Restore a checkout that contains the reviewer tool
findings.whyItBreaks: The repository tree at HEAD has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, or src/cli.ts. After the changed checkout, the install at line 51 and CLI invocation at line 59 run from that checkout, so pnpm cannot locate a manifest and the reviewer entrypoint is absent.

findings.title: Do not execute the PR checkout as the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed install and CLI commands execute from the checked-out PR head. workflow_dispatch bypasses the same-repository guard at line 24, accepts an arbitrary PR number, resolves that PR's head SHA, and checks it out. A maintainer can therefore dispatch this for a fork PR, causing its package install scripts or src/cli.ts to run on the self-hosted runner with GH_TOKEN configured for pull-request writes.

findings.title: Restore a trusted checkout for the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed checkout at lines 43-47 fetches the PR head into the workspace, and lines 49-59 install and execute its package dependencies and src/cli.ts while exposing GH_TOKEN. The workflow grants pull-requests: write and checks: write permissions, so an internal PR can alter the CLI or install lifecycle configuration to publish deceptive results or suppress findings. The base workflow instead ran a main-branch tool checkout against the PR target.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer executable on a trusted revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed checkout places the same-repository PR head in the workspace, then the changed install and review commands execute its package scripts, tsx binary, and src/cli.ts. A PR can alter those files and execute arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner with the workflow's pull-request and checks write-scoped GH_TOKEN.

findings.title: Restore a checkout that contains the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: HEAD contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json, so it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, node_modules, or src/cli.ts. The changed commands therefore cannot install the project or resolve the tsx binary and CLI, causing every review job to fail before producing a review.

findings.title: Preserve case-and-whitespace normalization for severity
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview maps untyped runtime findings through normalizeFinding. Values such as " p2 " or "p2" previously normalized to P2, but the new exact membership check emits P3 instead, silently lowering their priority.

findings.title: Preserve canonicalization before checking severity
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview maps raw findings through normalizeFinding. Values previously accepted after canonicalization, such as "p0" or " P0 ", now fail the exact enum check and are emitted as P3, silently downgrading high-severity findings.

findings.title: Restore canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview maps untyped parsed finding objects through normalizeFinding. Inputs previously accepted as valid severities, such as "p0" or " P2 ", now fail the exact-match check and are emitted as P3, downgrading a critical finding to the lowest severity.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `env` makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The base revision explicitly removed these credentials before launching `codex exec`; the child process and tools it invokes can now access them.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit `env` option makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, exposing `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN` to the prompt-driven Codex subprocess. The base revision explicitly removed these credentials.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the `env` option at the changed spawn call makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The prompt-driven `codex exec` subprocess can read those credentials; `-s read-only` does not restrict environment-variable access.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed job predicate allows fork pull requests to run. The job checks out the fork-controlled PR SHA, runs `pnpm install`, and executes the checked-out `src/cli.ts` on `runs-on: self-hosted`, allowing a fork author to execute arbitrary commands on that runner.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing this job-level condition allows fork PRs to run on the self-hosted runner. The workflow checks out the fork-controlled head SHA, then runs `pnpm install` and `tsx src/cli.ts`, so a fork author can execute arbitrary commands in the runner environment.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before executing PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now reach checkout of the attacker-controlled head SHA, then run both pnpm install and src/cli.ts on a self-hosted runner. A fork author can change package metadata or the CLI to execute arbitrary commands in the runner environment; the removed predicate previously prevented this.

findings.title: Keep zero-duration runner timeout settings valid
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed predicate rejects finite zero values that the prior parser accepted. With NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS="0", the configured immediate SIGKILL falls back to 5000 ms; NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS="0" falls back to 2000 ms instead of completing immediately.

findings.title: Keep zero-valued runner delays valid
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing deployments setting either NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 previously received an immediate timer. After upgrade, the same valid configuration silently becomes the 5000 ms or 2000 ms fallback, delaying SIGKILL escalation or completion.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner timeout settings
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" was previously accepted and passed to setTimeout, allowing immediate SIGKILL escalation or immediate give-up after SIGKILL. This change rejects it and silently substitutes 5000ms or 2000ms, so deployments using zero now wait several seconds instead.

findings.title: Retain coverage for changed files outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapped hotspots are now reviewed. Changed files absent from those selected hotspots never reach the deep-review loop, so defects in them can be omitted from the final verdict.

findings.title: Keep partial review results when one deep pass fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed deep-review response now rejects the exported review() call at the first failing hotspot, discarding prior findings. Previously the failure was emitted as a blocking residual risk and remaining hotspots continued.

findings.title: Propagate residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Successful deep-review residual risks are replaced with an empty array before candidateMerged is passed to the critic. A blocking risk produced by a deep review is therefore unavailable to the final critic/verdict path.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapped hotspots are reviewed. The removed tail hotspot was the sole path that added changed files omitted by those selected hotspots, so a valid mapper result with more than six disjoint hotspots silently omits the remaining files from findings and checked evidence.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep review can report a blocking residual risk, but this replacement always serializes an empty residual_risks array to the critic. The critic and final verdict therefore cannot distinguish a clean deep pass from one that was explicitly unresolved, and may return an unblocked result.

findings.title: Deep-review files excluded by the hotspot cap
findings.whyItBreaks: For large bundles, only the first six hotspots are reviewed. Removing the tail-coverage hotspot means any changed file omitted by the mapper or belonging only to a seventh-or-later hotspot is never deep-reviewed; the final critic receives only patchStat, so it cannot recover changed-line evidence for that file and can return a passing review despite an uninspected change.

findings.title: Preserve deep-pass residual risks for the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Successful deep passes can return blocking residual risks, but this code replaces them with []. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a fully reviewed bundle from one with unresolved blocking evidence and may emit a verdict that omits the block.

findings.title: Preserve focus for large-patch reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path drops `bundle.focus` from the map payload and removes its interpolation into each deep-review prompt. As a result, a caller-supplied review focus affects small patches but not large ones, so large-review findings can ignore the requested scope.

findings.title: Forward focus to the large-review deep pass
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed code removes bundle.focus from both the map payload and each deep-review prompt. Calls routed through review() to reviewLarge therefore cannot apply a caller-provided focus instruction, unlike reviewSmall, which serializes the full Bundle.

findings.title: Normalize rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed calculation derives minutes before rounding the remainder. At 119500ms it produces "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s"; at 59500ms it produces "60s" instead of "1m 0s".

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes before formatting
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119,600 ms, minutes is floored to 1 while the 59,600 ms remainder rounds to 60, so the rendered result is `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. This is shown to users in the review timing summary.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations from 119500ms through 119999ms, this computes `minutes = 1` and `seconds = 60`, rendering `1m 60s` instead of the normalized `2m 0s`. The prior implementation rounded before deriving minutes and did not produce this representation.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed condition accepts `0`, although the exported function name and its error contract promise a positive integer. Callers can now receive zero after relying on this parser for validation.

findings.title: Reject zero for positive integers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parsePositiveInteger function now returns 0, although both its name and thrown-error contract promise a positive integer. Consumers relying on this validator can pass zero into options that require a strictly positive value.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger` and its error text promise a positive integer, but `0` now passes the changed guard and is returned. This exported API therefore gives callers an invalid result for its documented validation contract.
